opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a fair concern, and it's one I take pretty seriously. LEACE, at its core, needs you to tell it what concept you want erased, and the way you do that is by providing labels: for each example, here's the value of the concept, say gender or part-of-speech or whatever. From those labels we compute the cross-covariance between the representations and the concept, and that's what defines the subspace we project out. So the eraser is only ever as good as your labels.

That creates a few problems. One is just cost and coverage. For a lot of concepts you'd actually care about erasing, you don't have a nice clean labeled dataset lying around, and building one is expensive. Another is that labels encode a particular operationalization of the concept. If your labels for "gender" are based on pronouns in the text, then what you erase is the linear information predictive of pronoun-based gender in *that* distribution. It may not generalize to other ways the concept shows up, and if your dataset has spurious correlations, you might erase something adjacent to what you meant, or miss parts of what you meant.

There's also a distribution shift issue. The guarantee LEACE gives is real: no linear classifier can recover the concept better than a constant predictor, but that guarantee holds with respect to the distribution you estimated the statistics on. Move to a different domain and the covariance structure can change, and some linearly decodable information can creep back.

That said, I'd push back a little on calling it purely a weakness. Some supervision is kind of unavoidable if you want to target a specific concept. An unsupervised method has to somehow figure out *which* direction you care about, and there's no free lunch there. So I see labels as the price of precision. The interesting research direction is reducing how much you need: using fewer labels, weak or noisy labels, labels generated by the model itself, or contrastive pairs instead of full annotations. Methods that find concept directions with minimal supervision, and then use something like LEACE to do the erasure cleanly with guarantees, are a pretty promising combination.

r001.rationale: The response says LEACE needs labels specifying the concept to erase and that those labels determine the cross-covariance used to define the subspace projected out.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think that's a fair criticism, and honestly it's probably the biggest practical limitation of the method as it stands.

So just to set the stage: LEACE, and really all of the concept erasure methods in this family, going back to INLP and R-LACE and so on, assume that you have a dataset where each example comes with a label for the concept you want to erase. Gender, part of speech, sentiment, whatever it is. LEACE then gives you a closed-form affine transformation that guarantees no linear classifier can recover that label better than chance, while perturbing the representations as little as possible. That guarantee is really nice. But it's a guarantee about the labels you gave it, not about the concept as it exists in the world.

And that distinction matters in a few ways. First, the labels have to actually track the thing you care about. If your gender labels are noisy, or if they're derived from pronouns in a way that only captures part of the concept, then you're erasing the thing your labels measure, which may not be the thing you intended to erase. The method can't tell the difference. It's only as good as your operationalization of the concept.

Second, there's the coverage issue. If your labeled data comes from one distribution, say a particular genre of text, you've computed the class-conditional means and the covariance structure on that distribution. There's no reason in principle that the same linear direction encodes the concept out of distribution, or that the covariance looks the same. So you can get a clean erasure on your held-out set and then find the concept is partially recoverable elsewhere. We've seen some of that empirically.

Third, and this is the one I find more interesting from a research standpoint, is that labeling presupposes you already know what the concept is and that it's cleanly categorical. A lot of the things we might want to erase, or that we'd want to study for interpretability reasons, don't come pre-packaged that way. The model may have carved up the world along axes that don't correspond to any human label we'd think to collect. So a method that requires labels is, in a sense, only going to let you erase concepts you already understood well enough to annotate. That's a real ceiling on what the tool can do.

Now, I'd push back a little on treating this as a flaw unique to LEACE. Any supervised probing or intervention method has the same dependency. And there are reasons to want it: labels are what let you make a precise, quantifiable claim about what was removed. If you go fully unsupervised, you lose that, and you often end up with something that's harder to interpret and harder to evaluate.

That said, I do think the natural direction is to relax the dependence. You could imagine using weak or noisy labels, or using pseudo-labels from another model, and then trying to characterize how the guarantee degrades as label quality degrades. Or you can go the other way and try to discover candidate directions unsupervised, with something like sparse dictionary learning, and then use LEACE-style machinery to intervene on them once you've found something you can name. In that setup the labels are more of a verification tool than the thing driving the whole procedure. I think that's probably where things are headed, but we're not there yet, and I don't want to oversell it. Right now, if you don't have good labels for the concept, LEACE isn't going to help you much.

r001.rationale: The response says LEACE erases the thing its labels measure and is only as good as the concept’s operationalization, making labeled data define the target.

astra-6.text:
Yeah, I think that’s a real limitation. With LEACE, you need labels for the concept you want to erase. So you might have a huge amount of text, but if you want to remove information about something like sentiment, you need some way of identifying sentiment in the data you use to fit the eraser.

And the guarantee is relative to those labels and that distribution. If your labels capture only part of what you mean by the concept, removing linear information about them doesn’t establish that you’ve removed the whole concept. It also doesn’t rule out a nonlinear model recovering information.

You could use another model to generate labels, which makes the annotation problem more manageable, but then you inherit that model’s mistakes and assumptions. So I’d see concept erasure as a useful, precise intervention when you have a well-defined target, rather than a general way to say, ‘Remove this abstract idea from the model.’

r001.rationale: The candidate says LEACE needs labels for the concept to erase and that its guarantee is relative to those labels, making clear that the labels define the target.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, I think that’s a real limitation. LEACE needs labels for the concept you want to erase, so you have to be able to operationalize that concept and get representative examples. For something like part of speech, that’s relatively straightforward. For something like truthfulness or harmfulness, it’s much less clear what the labels should mean.

And the guarantee is relative to those labels and the distribution you estimate the relevant statistics on. If your labels miss some aspect of the concept, or the distribution changes, you shouldn’t interpret the result as saying that the concept has been removed in every possible sense. In particular, LEACE removes linear information about the labeled concept; that doesn’t rule out nonlinear ways of recovering it.

So I’d view it as a precise tool for a fairly specific intervention. The dependence on labels limits where you can apply it, and it makes the quality of the concept definition really important.

r001.rationale: The response says LEACE needs labels for the concept to erase and that the concept must be operationalized, making the labels define the target.
